\chapter{Here, There, and Where}
\label{ch:bn-here-there-and-where}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say something is here or there, ask where it is, and deny that it is anywhere at all.}

The nine-cell grid closes: three heads — near, far, asking — across three frames — thing, person, place. The last cell is \bn{কোথায়}, the question an A1 candidate is asked in the first minute of a speaking test, and answering it needs the letter \bn{থ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[thô]{\bn{থ} — the breathy dental}

\label{lesson:BN-W05-tha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{ত}}, \textbf{\bn{খ}} and \textbf{\bn{ধ}}. Say what \textbf{\bn{খ}} has that \textbf{\bn{ক}} has not.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the ending that marks the person a thing is done to — \emph{-ke}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{থ}
\end{quote}

Six chapters ago you filled in the fourth corner of a square. This is a different square, and it has been three-quarters full for even longer.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{with breath} \\
\midrule
\textbf{voice off} & \textbf{\bn{ত}} \emph{tô} & \textbf{\bn{থ}} \emph{thô} \\
\textbf{voice on} & \textbf{\bn{দ}} \emph{dô} & \textbf{\bn{ধ}} \emph{dhô} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All four are made in the same place: the tongue flat on the back of the top front teeth. What separates them is the two switches — the voice, and the puff of breath you learned to hear when \textbf{\bn{খ}} arrived beside \textbf{\bn{ক}}.

\textbf{\bn{থ}} is the puff on the voiceless one. Hold a hand in front of your mouth: for \textbf{\bn{ত}} the air barely moves, for \textbf{\bn{থ}} it pushes.

And it is \textbf{not} the \emph{th} of English \emph{this} or \emph{thin}. That sound does not exist in Bengali. \textbf{\bn{থ}} is a \emph{t} with breath after it, nothing more.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{থ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{ত}} then \textbf{\bn{থ}} — same place, breath added
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole square — \textbf{\bn{ত} \bn{থ} \bn{দ} \bn{ধ}}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{থা}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ট} \bn{থ} — the two letters this book waited longest for
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \textbf{\bn{থ}} made? (\textbf{On the teeth}, like \textbf{\bn{ত}}.) What is added? (\textbf{Breath}.) Is it the English \emph{th}? (\textbf{No} — that sound is not in Bengali.) And which letter is its voiced partner? (\textbf{\bn{ধ}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ekhāne]{\bn{এখানে} (ekhāne) — here}

\label{lesson:BN-C26-ekhane}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{থ}}. Then say \textbf{this shirt}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{এখানে}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{এখানে}} — \emph{chā ekhāne} — \textbf{the tea is here.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সে} \bn{এখানে}} — \emph{she ekhāne} — \textbf{he is here.}
\end{quote}

Thirty-six chapters, and nothing in this book has had a \textbf{place}. Things could be named, pointed at, counted, owned and acted upon, and not one of them could be said to be anywhere.

\textbf{\bn{এখানে}} takes the near head \textbf{\bn{এ}-} you have owned since chapter thirty-two and puts it on a frame that means \emph{place}. And as with \textbf{\bn{এটা} \bn{জল}}, there is no verb in the middle: the thing, then where it is, and stop.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the grid, now in three dimensions}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{head} & \textbf{frame} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & thing & \textbf{\bn{এটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & person & \textbf{\bn{এ}} \\
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & place & \textbf{\bn{এখানে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & thing & \textbf{\bn{ওটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & person & \textbf{\bn{ও}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & place & \emph{next lesson} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & thing & \textbf{\bn{কী}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & person & \textbf{\bn{কে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & place & \emph{the lesson after} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nine cells, three heads, three frames. You have met seven of the nine, and the last two arrive in the next two lessons — which is the whole reason the pointing chapter was worth its five lessons.

And the denial is already yours: \textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{এখানে} \bn{নেই}} — \emph{the tea is not here} — using the \textbf{\bn{নেই}} of chapter twenty-seven, which denies existence rather than identity.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chā ekhāne}
  \item \emph{she ekhāne}, then \emph{āmi ekhāne}
  \item the denial — \emph{chā ekhāne nei}
  \item with the classifier — \emph{chāṭā ekhāne}
  \item the near head on all three frames — \emph{eṭā}, \emph{e}, \emph{ekhāne}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which head is inside \textbf{\bn{এখানে}}? (\textbf{\bn{এ}-}, the near one.) Is there a word for \emph{is} in \textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{এখানে}}? (\textbf{No}.) And which word denies it? (\textbf{\bn{নেই}} — the one that denies existence.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[okhāne]{\bn{ওখানে} (okhāne) — there}

\label{lesson:BN-C26-okhane}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{the tea is here}. Then say \textbf{that shirt}. Now guess this lesson's word before you read it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ওখানে}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সে} \bn{ওখানে}} — \emph{she okhāne} — \textbf{he is there.}
\end{quote}

If you guessed it, that is the lesson. Swap the head and cross the room, exactly as \textbf{\bn{এই}} became \textbf{\bn{ওই}} five chapters ago. The frame does not change; only the first letter does.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{এখানে}} — here, where I am
  \item \textbf{\bn{ওখানে}} — there, where I am not
\end{itemize}

Two places, as there were two distances. Bengali does not add a third.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: eight of nine}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{head} & \textbf{frame} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & place & \textbf{\bn{এখানে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & place & \textbf{\bn{ওখানে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & thing & \textbf{\bn{এটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & thing & \textbf{\bn{ওটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & thing & \textbf{\bn{কী}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & person & \textbf{\bn{কে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & place & \emph{one cell left} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Eight cells filled. The ninth is the next lesson, and it is the question an A1 examiner asks in the first minute of a speaking test.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{she okhāne}
  \item the pair — \emph{āmi ekhāne}, \emph{she okhāne}
  \item the denial — \emph{she okhāne nei}
  \item a whole group over there — \emph{bôndhurā okhāne}
  \item the far head on all three frames — \emph{oṭā}, \emph{o}, \emph{okhāne}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the only difference between \textbf{\bn{এখানে}} and \textbf{\bn{ওখানে}}? (\textbf{The head} — near against far.) How many places does Bengali distinguish? (\textbf{Two}.) And which cell of the grid is still empty? (\textbf{The asking one, for place}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kothāy]{\bn{কোথায়} (kothāy) — where?}

\label{lesson:BN-C26-kothay}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{here} and \textbf{there}. Then ask \textbf{who?}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{কোথায়}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তুমি} \bn{কোথায়}?} — \emph{tumi kothāy?} — \textbf{where are you?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জামাটা} \bn{কোথায়}?} — \emph{jāmāṭā kothāy?} — \textbf{where is the shirt?}
\end{quote}

The ninth cell, and the grid is closed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{head} & \textbf{frame} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & thing & \textbf{\bn{এটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & person & \textbf{\bn{এ}} \\
\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near & place & \textbf{\bn{এখানে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & thing & \textbf{\bn{ওটা}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & person & \textbf{\bn{ও}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ও}-} far & place & \textbf{\bn{ওখানে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & thing & \textbf{\bn{কী}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & person & \textbf{\bn{কে}} \\
\textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking & place & \textbf{\bn{কোথায়}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three heads, three frames, nine words — and you were shown the first head six chapters ago and have been filling the table in ever since.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question and its answer are the same shape}]
Ask down the bottom row and answer up the two rows above it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তুমি} \bn{কোথায়}?} — \textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{এখানে}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{এটা} \bn{কী}?} — \textbf{\bn{এটা} \bn{চা}}
\end{quote}

The same \textbf{\bn{ক}-} opens \textbf{\bn{কখন}}, which chapter thirty showed you inside a table of three heads without ever making it a word you could use. The grid was there before the words were.

Note the spelling: \textbf{\bn{কোথায়}} ends in \textbf{\bn{য়}}, the dotted \textbf{\bn{য}}, and it is a glide, not a \emph{j}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tumi kothāy?} — and answer — \emph{āmi ekhāne}
  \item \emph{jāmāṭā kothāy?} — and answer — \emph{jāmāṭā okhāne}
  \item the three questions of the bottom row — \emph{eṭā ki?}, \emph{ke?}, \emph{kothāy?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which head opens \textbf{\bn{কোথায়}}? (\textbf{\bn{ক}-}, the asking one.) Which two words answer it? (\textbf{\bn{এখানে}} and \textbf{\bn{ওখানে}}.) And what letter does it end in? (\textbf{\bn{য়}}, the dotted one — a glide.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ekhāne · okhāne · kothāy]{Here, there, and where}

\label{lesson:BN-R26-here-there-where}



\begin{quote}
Three heads and three frames make nine words. Say the whole grid out loud, one row at a time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{থ}, then \bn{ট}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tumi kothāy?} — \emph{āmi ekhāne} — \emph{she okhāne}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the denial — \emph{chā ekhāne nei}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the ending that marks the one a thing is done to — \emph{-ke}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the whole tranche, cold}
Seven chapters ago this book could not write the letter \textbf{\bn{ট}}, could not say \textbf{the} or \textbf{a}, could not make a plural, could not name a third person, could not mark who a thing was done to, and could not put anything anywhere. Run all of it, cold, from memory.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the classifier and its two doors — \emph{jāmāṭā}, \emph{ekṭā jāmā}, \emph{ārekṭā jāmā}
  \item the pointing pair, and both ends at once — \emph{ei jāmāṭā}, \emph{oi jāmāṭā}
  \item the question that decides the plural — is it \textbf{\bn{জীব}} or \textbf{\bn{জিনিস}}?
  \item the two plurals — \emph{bhāirā}, \emph{bônerā}; \emph{jāmāgulo}, \emph{nākgulo}
  \item an adjective that never changes — \emph{shôbuj jāmā}, \emph{shôbuj jāmāgulo}
  \item the six persons — \emph{āmi, āmrā, tumi, tomrā, she, tārā} — and the careful ones, \emph{āpni, tini}
  \item whose — \emph{āmār}, \emph{tār}, \emph{āmāder}, \emph{tāder}
  \item to whom — \emph{āmāke}, \emph{tomāke}, \emph{tāke}, \emph{bhāike}
  \item the three questions — \emph{eṭā ki?}, \emph{ke?}, \emph{kothāy?}
  \item and where things are — \emph{bhātṭā ekhāne}, \emph{chāṭā okhāne}, \emph{āmāder pôribār ekhāne}
  \item the longest phrase this book can now build — \emph{āmāder ei shôbuj jāmāṭā okhāne}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three heads? (\textbf{\bn{এ}-} near, \textbf{\bn{ও}-} far, \textbf{\bn{ক}-} asking.) What are the three frames? (\textbf{Thing}, \textbf{person}, \textbf{place}.) One question chose the plural, the classifier and the object ending — what was it? (\textbf{Is the noun alive?}) And which two letters had to be taught before any of these seven chapters could be written? (\textbf{\bn{ট}} and \textbf{\bn{থ}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
